results.message: What was a sermon like at Hippo?

voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
A sermon at Hippo was the regular work of a man answerable for his people. Augustine preached to the whole church, baptized or still learning, again and again, and it was the main way what we held reached an ordinary believer. He spoke to their faces, naming what he thought they needed. It was not a performance set apart from the rest of the service. It was the shepherd working on the flock placed in his care. That noise and those tears belong to the same bond the sermon served. He was given a people, not dropped into a posting, and he would be asked what became of them. Years later, already a bishop, he told his own congregation what that charge meant. Augustine says his hearers are in his care so he can give account for them, and that he wept when not heard: “You share communion with the members of the Apostles. You share communion with the shrines of the holy martyrs, who are spread over the whole world. And you belong to my care, so that I may give a good account of you. You know what my whole account is. ‘Lord, You know that I have spoken. You know that I have not kept silent. You know in what spirit I have spoken. You know that I have wept before You when I spoke and was not heard.’”

The sermon was where that accounting happened, week by week, in the open.

glosses.plain_meaning: A bishop, for us, is not an officer of some wider institution, dropped into a posting. He is given a people. He preaches to them and baptizes them, and when they fail it is not a problem he manages but a wound he carries. The charge runs both ways: he answers for his flock, and his flock can stand in front of his seat and refuse to leave until he hears them.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, the flock is not the church in general. It is the particular people one bishop is given, in one place. He answers for them, and they can hold him to it.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener often hears 'flock' as soft and a little patronizing -- pious language for churchgoers, gentle on the pastor's side, passive on theirs, and 'bishop' as a regional administrator several removes from ordinary life. We do not mean either. The flock is a charge that can be lost, and its failure is reckoned to the one who holds it. Our people are not passive: they elect, they demand, and they can force a bishop's hand. And the bishop is not remote -- he is the man who preached to you himself and knows which of you did not come.
false_friend: a soft, sentimental way of describing churchgoers, with a passive congregation and a gently benevolent pastor
a bishop understood as a remote regional administrator rather than the man who preaches to these people himself and knows who did not come

glosses.plain_meaning: For us, communion is a formal standing within the one body. You can lose it, and be given it back. At the council of 256, Cyprian said no one would be put out of it for thinking differently.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, communion is a real standing inside the one body. You can lose it, and be given it back. Cyprian held that it should survive sharp disagreement.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener is likely to hear either a specific liturgical rite -- going up to receive -- or a general warmth of fellowship, and the second makes disagreement look like a failure of communion. We mean a formal, structural status of standing within the body, with public consequences, that, on Cyprian's own principle, disagreement should not dissolve. Disagreement is expected among us; what would break communion is not arguing but separating.
false_friend: a specific liturgical rite alone, going up to receive, with no broader sense of standing attached
a general warmth of fellowship and mutual good feeling, so that any real disagreement looks like a failure of it

names.name: Augustinius of Hippo Regius, presbyter 391, bishop 395/396-430

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop at Hippo. The people seized him and brought him to be made a presbyter while he wept. Later they pressed him into the bishop's office over his own refusal. He spent his last days weeping over psalms of penitence, while an army lay outside the walls.

dates.display: converted 386, baptised 387; seized by the congregation at Hippo and ordained presbyter against his own wishes in 391, weeping through it (Possidius, Vita IV); designated coadjutor and consecrated bishop of Hippo by Megalius, primate of Numidia, in 395/396, again amid popular acclamation (Possidius, Vita VIII); died 430, during the Vandal siege of Hippo

confidence.divergence_note: The dense verbal evidence for this term is Cyprian's own; Augustine's use of the same image is real but far less frequent. Our claim that this is a cross-phase pattern rests on both bishops' own conduct of the office, not on matching word-counts in each phase (Author-Gravity-Risk: Yes, Lexicon_Deployment_Index.md SS6).

The chunk's own Key Sources section states this precisely rather than leaving it to inference: 'The underlying primary-source facts reach Documented. The synthesis -- that these constitute one named cross-phase gravity rather than two separate historical facts -- is this build's own reasoning, at Widely Accepted, and Doc_04 SS3 flags the divergence rather than upgrading it.' This term record IS that synthesis, so its own formation_confidence follows the synthesis's own rating, not the underlying quoted facts' rating. Doc_03 itself characterizes the pattern the same way: inferred from both bishops' conduct across more than one text, not a term either bishop names as such.

The text field is the NPNF English as printed. modern_rendering follows the Latin of PL 38 where the English misleads: 'memories of the Holy Martyrs' renders memoriis, which in African Latin of this period names a martyr's shrine or memorial chapel, and 'cure' renders curam, which here means care or charge.
